summary: Defines BUNDLE, an extension to the Session Description Protocol that lets several media streams, such as audio and video, share a single transport connection instead of using one each. It builds on the SDP offer/answer mechanism and adds related RTP Control Protocol items. Sharing a connection reduces the number of ports and NAT or firewall pinholes needed. It obsoletes RFC 8843.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending each toy in its own truck, you load them all into one truck. Fewer trucks need to cross the road.

questions: how to send audio and video over one port
what is the mid rtp header extension
subtitle: How two endpoints agree to carry audio, video and data over one shared network connection instead of one each.

tldr.problem: When each media stream in a call gets its own transport (5-tuple), every one consumes extra resources, especially when ICE is used to find working paths.
tldr.mechanism: BUNDLE is an SDP grouping extension used with offer/answer: it names the m= sections that will share one transport, picks one tagged section whose address and attributes apply to all, and adds a MID identifier so received RTP and RTCP can be matched to the right section.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9143 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8843, fixing an inconsistency in how port values are assigned, and updates RFC 3264, RFC 5888 and RFC 7941.

today: RFC 9143 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8843 and updates RFC 3264, RFC 5888 and RFC 7941. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Share One Transport
sections.content:
When the SDP offer/answer mechanism of RFC 3264 sets up a multimedia session, giving each media stream its own transport (5-tuple) is costly, especially when ICE is used. Sharing one transport is attractive.

This RFC defines the BUNDLE extension to the SDP Grouping Framework. It negotiates a single BUNDLE transport for the media described by several m= sections, which together form a BUNDLE group. One set of ICE candidates serves the whole group, and all RTP-based media in a group belong to a single RTP session. The mechanism only applies to SDP used with offer/answer; declarative use is out of scope.

BUNDLE is backward compatible. Endpoints that do not support it generate offers and answers without a group:BUNDLE attribute and give each m= section its own address and port.
sections.eli5: A phone call with sound and picture usually needs a separate road for each. BUNDLE lets them share one road so there is less to set up.

sections.title: Key Terms: Tags, Groups and Addresses
sections.content:
An m= section is one media description in an SDP body. Each carries an identification-tag in its mid attribute, and the BUNDLE group lists those tags in a group:BUNDLE attribute. The first tag in the list is the BUNDLE-tag: it points at the tagged m= section (offerer-tagged in an offer, answerer-tagged in an answer).

The tagged section matters because its address:port becomes the BUNDLE address:port and its IDENTICAL and TRANSPORT category attributes, called the BUNDLE attributes, apply to every section in the group. Section order in the tag list does not have to match the order of the sections in the SDP. A given section MUST NOT be in more than one group at a time, and the same BUNDLE transport is used for sending and receiving.

The bundle-only attribute is a media-level property with no value. Combined with a zero port, it asks the answerer to accept the section only if it supports BUNDLE and keeps the section in the group.
sections.eli5: Each stream wears a name tag. One stream is chosen as the group leader, and the leader's address and settings are used by everybody in the group.

sections.title: Negotiating a BUNDLE Group
sections.content:
In the initial BUNDLE offer the offerer gives each bundled section a unique address:port, except bundle-only sections, picks a suggested offerer-tagged section, puts all tags in the group:BUNDLE list with the suggested one first, and includes the BUNDLE attributes in every section except bundle-only ones. The suggested section MUST NOT be a bundle-only one, and it SHOULD be one the offerer believes is unlikely to be rejected or moved out.

The answerer checks the sections in tag order. It selects the first one that it will not move out of the group, will not reject and that has a non-zero port. That section becomes both the offerer-tagged section and, in the answer, the answerer-tagged section. If no section qualifies, the answerer MUST NOT create the group. The answerer assigns its BUNDLE address:port to every bundled section and lists them in its own group:BUNDLE attribute.

The offerer then applies the properties of the selected section to every bundled section. If the answer has no BUNDLE group, the offer is processed as a normal answer.
sections.eli5: One side suggests a group leader. The other side either agrees or picks the next one on the list, and then both sides use the leader's address for the whole group.

sections.title: Changing a Group After It Exists
sections.content:
Later offers can pick any bundled section as the offerer-tagged one, change the BUNDLE address:port, and add or remove attributes. Each offer must assign the BUNDLE address:port to the tagged section and to every other bundled section.

An offerer can add a section to the group, move it out by giving it a unique address:port and dropping its tag from the list, or disable it with a zero port and no bundle-only attribute. Moving a section from one group to another takes two offers. The answerer has fewer options: once a group exists, an answer cannot move a section out of it. An answerer can move a section out in the initial answer, or reject it with a zero port, but it cannot reject the offerer-tagged section in a subsequent exchange.

Because a subsequent offer is built by different rules from an initial one, a third-party call control that forwards a subsequent offer to a new endpoint SHOULD rewrite it into a valid initial BUNDLE offer.
sections.eli5: Players can join the group, leave it, or be switched off later. The leader cannot be kicked out by the other side in a single reply.

sections.title: RTP, ICE and DTLS in a Bundle
sections.content:
All RTP-based media in one group form a single RTP session, so they share one SSRC numbering space, and symmetric RTP MUST be used. A payload type can be reused across sections only if the codec configuration is identical. A given SSRC MUST NOT send packets using payload types from different sections. RTP and RTCP MUST be multiplexed on the same transport, and endpoints MUST support the rtcp-mux-only attribute.

Because the port no longer tells a receiver which section a packet belongs to, endpoints MUST support the MID mechanism. A receiver keeps tables mapping MIDs, SSRCs and unambiguous payload types to sections, and routes each RTP packet and each type of RTCP packet using them. Packets whose MID is not in the table are discarded.

With ICE, connectivity checks and keepalives only need to run for the BUNDLE transport. In an initial offer every section outside bundle-only ones carries unique ICE properties, while later only the tagged section carries them. With DTLS, there can be only one DTLS association per group, and a DTLS client that supports DTLS-SRTP MUST include the use_srtp extension.
sections.eli5: All the toys in the truck get name tags so the receiver can sort them into the right boxes, and only one lock and one set of road checks is needed.

sections.title: The MID Identifier in RTP and RTCP
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new RTCP SDES item, MID (Media Identification, value 15), and an RTP SDES header extension with the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:mid. Both carry the identification-tag as UTF-8 text that is not zero terminated. The header extension is enabled by an extmap attribute in every bundled RTP section in every offer and answer.

The MID SDES item SHOULD be sent in the first few RTCP packets after joining and regularly afterward. The header extension SHOULD be sent in some RTP packets at the start of a session and whenever the SSRC changes, and it may also help to include it in media access points such as video I-frames. The extension lets the recipient link media to the right section on the first decodable packet, even before the offerer has seen the answer.

Because the tag adds bytes to each packet, it is recommended to keep it short; a tag of 1 to 3 bytes uses the fewest 32-bit words with the one-byte header. The tag MUST NOT contain user information.
sections.eli5: Each packet carries a tiny sticker with the stream's name. Short stickers are best, because long ones take up room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BUNDLE does not change which information flows over the network, apart from the MID item. It changes which addresses and ports, and so which RTP sessions and security contexts, the information flows through, and it can make previously separate flows share one security context. Where different security policies would have applied to different streams, extra analysis is needed before choosing BUNDLE.

The identification-tag can be seen beyond the signaling chain, so it MUST be generated without leaking user information, for example randomly or with a per-group counter, and SHOULD be 3 bytes or fewer. Different generation methods could allow fingerprinting of an implementation. Because the tag routes media to the right application function, its integrity and source authenticity matter, and existing SRTP configurations protect them.

RFC 7941 requires a confidentiality-protected SDES header extension to be protected too. This RFC adds an exception: the requirement MAY be ignored for the MID header extension, since no significant security risk is known in leaving it unprotected.
sections.eli5: Putting everything in one truck means one lock covers everything, so check that is okay. The name stickers must not reveal who you are.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 8843
sections.content:
After RFC 8843 and RFC 8829 were published, an inconsistency between them was found in how the port value is assigned to a bundled section in answers and in subsequent offers. RFC 9143 aligns the procedure with RFC 8829. It also implements changes from two errata reports.

The practical difference is that RFC 8843 gave only the tagged section the BUNDLE address:port and marked every other section bundle-only with a zero port. The new text assigns the BUNDLE address:port to every bundled section. How a compliant endpoint handles old-style offers and answers is left to the implementation.
sections.eli5: The first edition used a shortcut that did not match another document. The second edition fixes it so both agree.

m=audio 10000 RTP/AVP 0 8 97
a=mid:foo
a=rtcp-mux
a=extmap:1 urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:mid

m=video 0 RTP/AVP 31 32
a=mid:bar
a=bundle-only
a=extmap:1 urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:mid
